security_spec.violation_condition: Kernel context-switch and KVM vCPU save/restore paths preserve fflags/fcsr without sanitization, transparently propagating implementation-defined fflags values produced by IME floating-point matrix multiply-accumulate instructions (vfmmacc.vv, vfwmmacc.vv, vfqwmmacc.vv). The intermediate grouping factor G and rounding order within a single instruction are implementation-defined and not governed by frm, so the resulting fflags bit pattern encodes the host microarchitecture's internal accumulation grouping. A userspace process or guest VM can probe fflags after IME instructions to fingerprint the host microarchitecture, distinguishing CPU implementations or cores in a heterogeneous system.
security_spec.summary: IME floating-point instructions produce implementation-defined fflags encoding microarchitectural grouping factor G, leaked through kernel fcsr save/restore across security boundaries

findings.finding: Correctly saves the complete fcsr CSR (which includes frm[7:5] and fflags[4:0]) via frcsr at line 27, then stores to the thread struct at line 60. The kernel must faithfully preserve all architectural fcsr state across context switches — a process may legitimately accrue exception flags, context-switch out, and expect them to be intact upon resume. Sanitizing fflags here would be a kernel bug, not a fix.

spec_citations.excerpt: The floating-point control and status register, fcsr, is a RISC-V control and status register (CSR). It is a 32-bit read/write register that selects the dynamic rounding mode for floating-point arithmetic operations and holds the accrued exception flags.

The accrued exception flags indicate the exception conditions that have arisen on any floating-point arithmetic instruction since the field was last reset by software. The base RISC-V ISA does not support generating a trap on the setting of a floating-point exception flag.

findings.finding: Correctly restores the complete fcsr CSR from the thread struct via fscsr at line 103. This is required for correct context-switch semantics — fflags values set by FP/vector instructions executed before the switch must survive the switch.

The switch_to macro correctly sequences FP then vector state save/restore before the GPR switch. fstate_save/restore use SR_FS tracking (DIRTY/CLEAN/OFF) to avoid unnecessary save/restore operations — this is the standard lazy FP optimization used across architectures. No sanitization is applied (nor should it be).

KVM guest FP save path reads fcsr via frcsr at line 320 and stores it to the kvm_cpu_context at line 353. Correctly preserves the full fcsr value including fflags. This is necessary for correct VM migration and save/restore semantics — if a guest accrued NX on a vfmacc instruction, the flag must survive VM exit and re-entry.

KVM guest FP restore path loads fcsr from kvm_cpu_context at line 403 and writes via fscsr at line 437. Correctly restores the full architectural FP state that was saved at VM exit. Sanitization here would corrupt guest-visible state.

VM entry sequence: host FP saved, guest FP restored. The ordering is correct and the save/restore faithfully preserves fcsr/fflags without sanitization — exactly what is needed for correct VM semantics.

VM exit sequence: guest FP saved, host FP restored. Correct order and correct state preservation. The guest's fflags are saved to the guest context and the host's fflags are restored — any other behavior would either leak host state to the guest (security bug) or corrupt the guest state (functional bug).

Correctly zeros the entire fstate struct (including fcsr/fflags) at exec() time. Comment at line 188 explicitly documents 'fflags: accrued exceptions cleared'. This is the right place to clear fflags — a new program image starts with clean FP state. The kernel does NOT clear fflags on regular context switch, which is also correct per spec.

spec_citations.excerpt: The accrued exception flags indicate the exception conditions that have arisen on any floating-point arithmetic instruction since the field was last reset by software.

findings.finding: CPU initialization zeros fcsr (clearing both frm and fflags) before enabling FPU. This ensures each CPU starts with deterministic FP state. The boot CPU and secondary CPUs both execute this path.

Sets guest sstatus.FS to INITIAL (a vCPU reset does not touch saved fcsr — that is implicitly zero from the kvm_cpu_context allocation). The guest's fcsr state is properly isolated in guest_context and never merged with host state.

Vector CSR save saves vstart, vtype, vl, vcsr, vlenb. For standard V, reads CSR_VCSR at line 162. For T-Head, assembles vcsr from VXSAT/VXRM. The vector VCSR does NOT alias fcsr/fflags — vector FP instructions set the scalar fflags in the fcsr CSR (per spec section 'Vector Floating-Point Exception Flags'), not in vcsr. The fcsr save/restore is handled independently by __fstate_save/restore.

spec_citations.excerpt: A vector floating-point exception at any active floating-point element sets the standard FP exception flags in the fflags register. Inactive elements do not set FP exception flags.

findings.finding: Signal delivery correctly saves vector state before copying to userspace. The FP state (including fcsr/fflags) is handled through the sigframe save path which calls fstate_save. Both FP and vector state are transparently written to the signal frame — this is correct: userspace has the right to inspect its own fflags via the signal frame (e.g., a signal handler might need to know whether the interrupted code produced inexact results).
